 USDA proposal would cut SNAP for 6.3 million more Americans 
 The rule would limit broad-based categorical eligibility, a policy Minnesota expanded in 2010. About 440,000 Minnesotans receive SNAP, and nearly 25% of SNAP participants nationally are Black. 
 by 
 Jennifer Porter Gore

 Proposed USDA Rule Would End SNAP Benefits for 6.3 Million People, Including Some Minnesotans
 The U.S. Department of Agriculture published a proposed rule Nov. 10 that would restrict broad-based categorical eligibility, which lets states extend SNAP to households receiving TANF-funded services such as child care help or job training. Only households getting TANF cash assistance would automatically qualify. The USDA estimates 6.3 million people would lose benefits by 2029. The agency calls the policy a loophole, while Rep. Jahana Hayes and hunger advocates say the rule targets vulnerable families. Minnesota, where about 440,000 people receive SNAP, uses the policy, so some households could lose benefits. Public comments are open through Dec. 10 at regulations.gov.
 Head Case Manager Gerice Williams and her team serve students lunch during PASS Program Thanksgiving Event Lunch at Kramer Middle School in Washington, DC, United States on November 25, 2024. Credit: Shedrick Pelt / The Washington Post via Getty Images 
 Exactly one week after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the U.S. Department of Agriculture is proposing a change to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program that it says would cause 6.3 million people to lose food assistance.

 The proposed rule, published Nov. 10 in the Federal Register, would restrict a policy called broad-based categorical eligibility. The policy lets states extend SNAP to households that receive benefits or services funded by Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, including non-cash help such as child care assistance or job training. Under the proposal, only households receiving TANF cash assistance would automatically qualify for SNAP. Everyone else would have to meet the program’s standard income and asset tests.
 According to a USDA impact analysis, about 17.6% of current SNAP participants would lose their benefits. That’s 3.2 million households containing 6.3 million people in fiscal year 2029, when the rule is expected to take full effect. The cuts would reduce federal benefit spending by roughly $44.6 billion over five years.
 “The newly released proposed rule once again targets the most vulnerable among us by narrowing eligibility and blocking families from vital food assistance,” Rep. Jahana Hayes, D-Conn., ranking member of the House Nutrition and Foreign Agriculture Subcommittee, said in a statement.
 The proposal comes as SNAP enrollment has already dropped by more than 5 million people, including an estimated 2 million children, since President Donald Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in July 2025, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.
 According to a 2024 USDA report, three-quarters of SNAP households had incomes at or below federal poverty guidelines, and most included a child, an older adult or a person with disabilities. Almost 25% of SNAP participants are Black.
 The Trump administration proposed a similar rule in 2019, which the Biden administration withdrew in 2021.
 “Broad-based categorical eligibility has bloated the welfare rolls for decades,” a USDA spokesperson said in a statement. “Correcting this loophole is long overdue.”
 Families who lose SNAP would also face a more complicated process to get free school meals and benefits through the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children, known as WIC. Just over 21% of WIC participants are Black.
 The USDA estimates that about 1.78 million children would no longer automatically qualify for free school meals, though it says almost all of them could still qualify based on household income through a separate process.
 Hunger prevention advocates say the current system cuts red tape and administrative costs while helping millions of children, disabled adults and working people with low incomes get fed.
 “It simply moves the cost of hunger off the federal ledger and onto food banks, pantries, school cafeterias and families,” Jenique Jones, executive director of WhyHunger, said in a statement. “This is not reform. This is a benefit cut dressed up as paperwork.”
 Minnesota is among the states that use broad-based categorical eligibility. In 2010, the Minnesota Legislature expanded the policy to all SNAP cases, raising the income limit from 130% to 165% of federal poverty guidelines and eliminating the asset limit, according to the state Department of Human Services, which ran the program at the time. That means some Minnesota households that now qualify could lose benefits if the rule takes effect.
 About 440,000 Minnesotans receive SNAP, according to the Minnesota Department of Children, Youth, and Families, which now runs the program. The department estimates that last year’s budget law alone will leave recipients with about $5 less per month on average in 2027 and make about 9,000 fewer Minnesotans eligible in an average month because of new citizenship restrictions.
 Minnesota also figures in the federal government’s case for the change. In the proposed rule, the USDA points to a widely cited case of a Minnesota millionaire who received food stamps through broad-based categorical eligibility.
 Minnesota students would continue to eat for free at school regardless, because the state has provided universal free school meals since 2023. But federal reimbursements depend partly on how many students are certified for free meals, so fewer automatically eligible students could shift more of the cost to the state.
 The public can submit comments through Dec. 10 at regulations.gov under docket number FNA-2026-0661, “Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program: Reforming Categorical Eligibility.” Comments can also be emailed to sm.fn.snappdbrules@usda.gov with the docket number in the subject line.
 This article appeared first in Word in Black. It has been edited for style and length, and  Minnesota Spokesman-Recorder contributed the Minnesota reporting. For the original, visit https://wordinblack.com/2026/11/usda-proposal-would-end-snap-benefits-for-6-3-million-more-americans/ .  
 Jennifer Porter Gore is a writer living in the Washington, D.C., area.
